From the perspective of someone not already invested in the manga: [h3]Light Fights In Tight Pages[/h3] For a manga themed roguelike deckbuilder, this is a thin read. 1 campaign, 3 characters and 2 difficulty modes are all you get for your $10.00. The shaped comic panels and divergent HP system is novel, but beyond that, it's difficult to justify a purchase beyond the stylish art (both panel and pixel). I'm glad I tried it, but were I asked to recommend an anime/manga themed roguelike deckbuilder, I'd probably sooner pitch WanderStars, Chrono Ark or Card-en-Ciel, provided you're not a stickler for the "like/lite" suffix.

[h3] 杀人要做专家 玩游戏同样也要做专家[/h3] 作为一个看过原著的玩家来说，这是一款很有诚意的粉丝向作品。 玩法非常新颖。 通过漫画分格的方式来构筑你的攻击动作，既有肉鸽的惊喜感也带有一点背包类游戏的构筑型。 小游戏还原了原作中的那些无厘头黑色幽默感，其中埋藏的漫画梗也是能让原作党会心一笑的程度。 但美中不足的诗作为肉鸽类随机性不够强，作为背包类深度又不够。 虽然三个角色特点不同，但是打专家的时候某个角色太坐牢了...[spoiler] 铃木你咋这么菜 [/spoiler] 而且因为内容深度不足导致的关卡重复性过高，很容易产生疲劳感。 所以解密模式反而可玩性更高。 UI虽然能看出有用心但美术太简陋了。 最重要的是...为啥没配音kora！ 那种好像从免费素材网站偷的音效太偷懒了kora！ 多做点关卡啊kora! 不过，我还是强烈安利给没有看过原作的玩家可以去看看动画。 看完以后或许就会有新的体验也说不定哦

I dig it. Interesting mechanics that are sort or a cross between adaptive puzzle and beat-em-up style fighting. Has enough differentiation from what I've played before that I actually like to think about it. It's almost a coding game where you program your character on the fly using random "cards" from your "deck". Are you into finding solutions to problems just so you can occupy your mind? This isn't a terrible way to do it, feels fresh and has some good humor to it. It reminds me of the first gameboy Wario minigames thing from forever ago. Probably better on sale at 50% off if this is strictly a value based proposition.

The Fable: Manga Build Roguelike is one of the more inventive strategy roguelikes to emerge from a manga adaptation because it transforms the identity of its source material directly into gameplay mechanics instead of simply borrowing characters and story elements. Developed by MONO ENTERTAINMENT and published by Kodansha, the game reimagines the world of The Fable as a tactical roguelike built entirely around arranging comic panels to create combat sequences. Rather than using traditional turn-based combat or standard deckbuilding systems, the game asks players to think like both a strategist and a manga editor, carefully constructing pages that determine movement, attacks, defense, and special actions. The result is a surprisingly clever blend of puzzle solving, tactical planning, and roguelike progression that feels genuinely different from most games in the genre. The core gameplay revolves around collecting and placing action panels onto comic-book pages during combat encounters. Each panel represents a specific action such as attacking, dodging, moving, blocking, or using special abilities. Once placed, the sequence executes automatically according to the layout players have created. This system immediately changes the flow of strategy because success depends not only on choosing the right actions but also on arranging them efficiently across limited page space. Every battle feels like building a carefully choreographed action scene where timing and placement matter just as much as raw power. One of the most impressive mechanics is how damage affects the comic pages themselves. When the player takes heavy hits, sections of the manga page become permanently destroyed for the duration of the encounter, reducing the available space where future panels can be placed. This mechanic constantly increases pressure during combat because mistakes physically limit strategic options over time. Players must adapt their plans around damaged pages while still finding ways to survive difficult encounters. It is an incredibly smart design decision because it ties the comic-book presentation directly into gameplay rather than treating the manga aesthetic as simple visual decoration. The tactical depth becomes much stronger as additional panels, upgrades, and characters are introduced throughout repeated runs. Different characters bring completely different combat styles and abilities into battle, encouraging experimentation with new page layouts and action sequences. Some characters excel at aggressive offensive chains, while others reward stealth, positioning, defensive planning, or mobility-focused strategies. Since every run introduces randomized upgrades and encounters, players are constantly adapting their approach based on available resources and panel combinations. The roguelike structure fits the game surprisingly well. Each run gradually expands the player’s tactical options through new panels, modifiers, and upgrades, creating a satisfying sense of progression without overwhelming players too quickly. Strong combinations can create devastating attack sequences capable of clearing enemies efficiently, while weaker or poorly planned layouts leave characters vulnerable. The game constantly rewards experimentation because discovering effective panel synergies is one of the most satisfying aspects of the experience. One of the game’s greatest strengths is how faithfully it captures the personality of The Fable manga itself. Fans of the original series will immediately recognize the awkward humor, bizarre character interactions, and sudden bursts of violence that defined the source material. The balance between absurd comedy and tense combat is handled surprisingly well. Quiet moments between missions often feature strange conversations and comedic side activities that contrast sharply with the intensity of combat encounters. This tonal balance prevents the game from becoming too mechanically repetitive while also helping it feel like a genuine extension of the manga rather than a generic licensed product. Visually, the game successfully combines manga-inspired layouts with retro pixel art and comic-book presentation. Character animations are expressive despite the pixel-based style, and the constantly changing comic page layouts give battles a unique visual identity. Watching action panels unfold across the page creates the feeling of controlling an interactive manga rather than a standard strategy game. The interface also remains relatively readable despite the complexity of later encounters, which is important because players often need to process large amounts of tactical information quickly. The soundtrack complements the experience nicely with energetic combat themes and more atmospheric tracks during quieter moments. Audio cues help reinforce successful attack chains and movement sequences, making carefully planned combos feel satisfying when executed correctly. While the soundtrack may not become especially memorable outside the game itself, it supports the pacing and overall atmosphere effectively. Another standout feature is the dedicated puzzle mode, which isolates the game’s strongest mechanics into focused combat scenarios. Instead of relying on randomized progression, these challenges ask players to solve carefully designed encounters using limited panels and strict tactical restrictions. Some of these puzzles become genuinely difficult and require extremely precise planning, making them a great addition for players who enjoy strategy games built around optimization and problem solving. However, the game is not without weaknesses. The learning curve can occasionally feel punishing, especially once page destruction mechanics and enemy complexity begin stacking together during later runs. Some encounters demand extremely careful planning and repeated experimentation, which may frustrate players looking for a more casual roguelike experience. Because every turn matters so heavily, longer sessions can also become mentally exhausting. Randomized progression sometimes creates uneven runs as well. Certain panel combinations are dramatically stronger than others, and unlucky upgrades or poor early offerings can leave players struggling to build effective strategies. While skill still plays a major role in survival, some runs feel noticeably harder simply because of weaker panel options. Balance issues occasionally make experimentation feel less rewarding once dominant strategies become obvious. The game’s unusual concept may also divide players. Strategy fans expecting traditional deckbuilding or tactical combat systems may initially struggle to adapt to the comic-page structure. In addition, players unfamiliar with The Fable manga may not fully appreciate some of the humor, references, or character dynamics that longtime fans will recognize immediately. Fortunately, the gameplay itself remains strong enough to stand on its own even without deep knowledge of the source material. Despite these flaws, The Fable: Manga Build Roguelike succeeds because it fully commits to its creative vision. The comic panel system fundamentally changes how players think about combat, and the integration between presentation and mechanics is genuinely impressive. Combined with strong tactical depth, replayable roguelike progression, and faithful adaptation of the manga’s atmosphere, the game delivers one of the more original strategy experiences released in recent years. For players who enjoy tactical puzzle games, roguelike progression systems, and unusual strategy mechanics, The Fable: Manga Build Roguelike offers a fresh and highly memorable experience. It may require patience to fully understand its systems, but once the mechanics click together, the game becomes an addictive mix of strategy, experimentation, and comic-book action that feels unlike almost anything else in the genre. Rating: 8/10

Good introduction to tile building board games, if you are interested at all in tile/deck and blind bag type games I think this would be worth your while. Has cute sub game filler which is well just filler but helps set the games feels. Overall a positive experience for me.

For the price, this game offers a good amount of well done content. The gameplay itself I find to be pretty satisfying, the roguelike elements gives it good re-playability as there's around 3 different build paths you can take per character. For example, the first character Akira has access to panels that focus on hand to hand combat, gunplay with his pistol, and defensive panels that allow you to avoid damage. You can try and go all in on any of those 3 playstyles however you always start with a predetermined deck specific to the character you selected that has a mix of the aforementioned playstyles. Meaning if you want to min-max your deck you not only need good RNG in pulling the right panels in rewards, but you also need to get rid of panels that don't suit your selected playstyle so you can more consistently draw into the ones you need. Luckily there's a mulligan option you can use once per battle incase you ever draw into a totally bricked hand. Speaking of the Manga panels in terms of gameplay, this is one of the games biggest strengths. Building a page from separate panels and ordering your moves for max efficiency is a genuine puzzle thats both interesting and rewarding to deduce. this is further reinforced by the diversity of enemies, as some will be melee only and need to walk up to you to hit you while others have range in the form of guns, and others can buff or give orders to power up their cohorts meaning you will want to prioritize the more dangerous enemies first above all else which can be tricky when they have a row or two of tanky melee meat shields between your target enemy and yourself. Taking any sort of damage is very detrimental, as the game doesn't incorporate a traditional health bar. Instead, taking damage makes it so that for each point of damage you take will make it so you also lose access to a part of your page meaning you can play less panels/cards per turn as you have less of the page to work with. This is compounded by the shape of the panels you receive as some will for example take an L shape and if even one of the squares on your page where you want to set the panel on is damaged will make it so you can no longer play the panel there which messes with how you can order them and of course how many you can set. Every battle gives you a predetermined amount of turns, and you need to eliminate all the enemies in that amount of turns or less , if not you lose. This makes it so whenever you take damage you can be seriously impaired in what you can do next turn, as you will have less of the page to work with and insert panels into, subsequently forcing you to take longer and longer to finish out fights. This is mitigated by a resource, tape funnily enough, which you get for successfully completing fights in a run and it can also be purchased at shops using a currency you also gain from winning fights. So it's not completely unforgiving. But let me say theres nothing more satisfying then composing a great looking page using all the right panels on all the right enemies. The amount of style the combat has isn't readily apparent due to the turn based nature of the game, however after each fight you are given the option to replay the fight as an almost cutscene playing out in real time. Making every minor dodge, punch, and shot you meticulously planned come together beautifully as you see your character deftly take out each enemy with smoking sick style. The base game mode is the roguelike with you going from stage to stage, including regular fight stages against various goons, reward stages which give you new panels to add to your deck, upgrade stages where you can pick 1 panel in your deck and increase its its stats (dmg or defenses depending on what the panel inherently does), store stages where you can buy more panels or delete ones you no longer need, straight up delete stages that only serve to thin your deck out by again removing panels you no longer need, and finally boss stages at the end of each level with each run consisting of 3 levels with each level being subsequently longer than the last. You also have minigame stages, almost forgot haha, which are basically like reward stages except you play a minigame and the better you do on the minigame the better rewards you get from those stages, usually in the form of new panels to add to your deck. The minigames are simple enough, and some are fun, though admittingly the minigames aren't really my thing personally but they aren't offensive either so im rather neutral on them. The boss fights introduce new mechanics which add a new challenge all while keeping you honest by requiring you to clear the fight in a predetermined amount of turns, I would have wished for more bosses, as it seems you always fight the same boss at the end of the level. Alternatively, there is also a puzzle mode where you are given a certain hand with certain panels against a certain set of enemies and asked to eliminate them in a turn or two making it so you have to figure out the optimal way to play your panels in order to eliminate the enemies fast enough to beat the turn limit. This takes the best part of the game and further plays on it, leaving me scratching my head at times as to how I can get the most value out of each panel, with quite a lot of "puzzle fights" available with a wide array of difficulties ranging from tough to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, no mistakes allowed. All in all, The Fable is a solid game the will keep you entertained for a couple of days before you've more or less seen all the content. Game is currently 10$ and on sale for 7$ USD. For the price, you really can't ask for more so if you like the way the game incorporates the manga panel element into its card game like gameplay id recommend picking it up, it also has a demo which gives you access to the first character Akira, you can run him through a few roguelike run in that game mode and you can also run through some of the puzzle battles so play the demo if you aren't sure, it'll let you try everything you'd need to in order to decide if you'd like the game or not.
